## Statement refuted

Every measurable statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ is a valid p-value for a
given null hypothesis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A statistical experiment with a nonempty null hypothesis and a
disjoint nonempty alternative, and the definition of a valid p-value.

[F1] [[def-statistical-experiment]]: an experiment supplies a measurable data space and a probability law for each parameter.

[F2] [[def-p-value]]: a valid p-value must satisfy $P_\theta(p(X)\le u)\le u$ for every null parameter and every $u\in[0,1]$.

[F3] [[def-test-size-and-power]]: for the simple null
$\Theta_0=\{\theta_0\}$ and a nonempty disjoint alternative, size is the
rejection probability under $P_{\theta_0}$.

[F4] [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]: a statistic is measurable when all measurable target sets have measurable preimages.

[F5] [[cor-expectation-of-an-indicator-is-probability]]: the expectation of an event indicator is the event's probability.

[F6] [[lem-measurable-rejection-function-defines-randomized-test]]: every measurable function into $[0,1]$ defines a binary randomized test.

## Counterexample

1.1 Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with the full sigma-algebra, $\Theta=\{\theta_0,\theta_1\}$, $\Theta_0=\{\theta_0\}$, and $\Theta_1=\{\theta_1\}$. Set $P_{\theta_0}(\{0\})=P_{\theta_0}(\{1\})=1/2$ and $P_{\theta_1}(\{0\})=0$, $P_{\theta_1}(\{1\})=1$. These masses define probability measures: they are nonnegative and sum to one, and on the two-point space countable additivity follows because at most two members of a disjoint family are nonempty. Define $p(0)=0$ and $p(1)=1$. It is measurable because every subset of $\mathcal X$ is measurable. [given, F1, F4, algebra, construct]

## Example

On $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra and counting measure
$\mu$, let the simple null and alternative laws be
$P_0(\{0\})=P_0(\{1\})=1/2$ and
$P_1(\{0\})=1/4$, $P_1(\{1\})=3/4$. At level $\alpha=1/4$, the
Neyman–Pearson test randomizes with probability $1/2$ at $x=1$ and rejects
with probability $0$ at $x=0$. Its size is $1/4$ and its power is $3/8$.

## Verification

**Given:** The two probability laws above, counting measure $\mu$, and
$\alpha=1/4$. Assume AC for the general Neyman–Pearson comparison.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: the Neyman–Pearson theorem is used in its
AC density-selection branch; the finite example's densities are explicit.

[F1] [[def-counting-measure]]: each singleton has $\mu$-measure $1$.

[F6] [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]] and [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]: the counting set function is a measure; a finite measure is sigma-finite.

[F2] [[def-likelihood-ratio-test-with-boundary-randomization]] and [[lem-likelihood-ratio-test-is-measurable-and-exact-size]]: the candidate is a measurable randomized test of exact size; on $\{p_0>0\}$ it rejects above its cutoff and randomizes by $\gamma$ at equality.

[F3] [[def-test-size-and-power]]: size is null rejection probability and power is alternative rejection probability.

[F4] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], and [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]: expectation of this finite-valued rejection function is the sum of its values weighted by the point masses.

[F5] [[thm-neyman-pearson-lemma]]: no test of size at most $1/4$ has larger power than the constructed likelihood-ratio test.

[F7] [[def-probability-measure]]: a measure with total mass $1$ is a probability measure.

[F8] [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]: every real-valued function on the two-point space with its full sigma-algebra is measurable.

1.1 By [F1] and [F6], $\mu$ is a measure with $\mu(\mathcal X)=2$, so it is finite and hence sigma-finite. Each displayed law has nonnegative masses summing to $1$, and any disjoint family of subsets of $\{0,1\}$ has at most two nonempty members, so each law is countably additive. Thus $P_0,P_1$ are probability measures by [F7]. [given, F1, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Define $p_0(0)=p_0(1)=1/2$, $p_1(0)=1/4$, and $p_1(1)=3/4$. They are finite, nonnegative, and measurable by [F8]. For every $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, the simple-integral formula in [F4] gives $\int_Ap_i\,d\mu=\sum_{x\in A}p_i(x)=P_i(A)$, so these are density representatives and $P_i\ll\mu$. Hence $R(0)=1/2$ and $R(1)=3/2$. With $c=3/2$, $P_0(R>c)=0$ and $P_0(R=c)=1/2$, so the boundary equation gives $\gamma=(1/4)/(1/2)=1/2$. The test has $\varphi^*(1)=1/2$ and $\varphi^*(0)=0$. [F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Using [F4], its size is $E_{P_0}\varphi^*=(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(0)=1/4$, and its power is $E_{P_1}\varphi^*=(3/4)(1/2)+(1/4)(0)=3/8$. Thus it uses the boundary atom to attain the requested size. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The Neyman–Pearson lemma [F5] makes this test most powerful among all tests whose size is at most $1/4$. [A1, F5, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every finite-mean law has a finite-variance influence curve for its mean functional in the dominated local model generated by bounded mean-zero score tilts.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The statement above and the definitions of DQM paths and parameter influence curves.

[F1] [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]: a one-sided common-dominated path is DQM when its square-root density has the stated first-order $L^2$ expansion.

[F2] [[def-pathwise-differentiable-functional]]: a finite-variance parameter influence curve is a vector in $L^2_0(P)$ representing path derivatives by the $L^2(P)$ pairing.

[F3] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]: $|P[fg]|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ for square-integrable $f,g$.

[F4] [[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]: if the second derivative is bounded on an interval, the first-order Taylor polynomial has a remainder bounded by a constant times the square of the displacement.

## Counterexample

**Given:** Let $\mathcal X=\mathbb N_{\ge1}$, $P\{j\}=2^{-j}$, $f(j)=2^{j/2}$, and $\psi(Q)=Qf$. Allow all local tilts $dP_{t,s}=(1+ts)dP$ with bounded $s$ satisfying $Ps=0$.

1.1 The masses sum to one. The geometric series gives $Pf=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}<\infty$, while $P[f^2]=\sum_{j\ge1}1=\infty$. Thus $\mu=Pf$ is finite and $u=f-\mu$ is integrable, centered, but not square-integrable. [given, algebra]

1.2 For any bounded centered $s$, choose $t\ge0$ so small that $|ts|\le1/2$ everywhere. Then $1+ts\ge0$ and $P(1+ts)=1$. On $[-1/2,1/2]$, $g(x)=\sqrt{1+x}$ has $g''(x)=-1/(4(1+x)^{3/2})$, so $|g''(x)|\le1$. [F4] with $n=1$ gives $\sqrt{1+ts}=1+\frac t2s+O(t^2\|s\|_\infty^2)$ uniformly; thus the tilt is DQM with score $s$. Since $f\in L^1(P)$ and $s$ is bounded, $\psi(P_{t,s})=Pf+tP[fs]$ and $\dot\psi_P(s)=P[us]$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

1.3 For $M>0$, put $u_M=u\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le M\}}$, $c_M=Pu_M$, and $s_M=u_M-c_M$. Then $s_M$ is bounded and centered, $D_M:=P[u^2\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le M\}}]=P[us_M]$, and $\|s_M\|_2^2=D_M-c_M^2\le D_M$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $u(j)\ge2^{j/2}/2$, so each such included atom contributes at least $1/4$ to $D_M$; as $M\to\infty$, arbitrarily many atoms are included and $D_M\to\infty$. For large $M$, $s_M\ne0$ because the truncation vanishes on a positive-mass tail and is nonzero on included atoms. Hence $|\dot\psi_P(s_M)|/\|s_M\|_2\ge\sqrt{D_M}\to\infty$. [given, algebra]

2.1 If a finite-variance influence curve $\phi\in L^2_0(P)$ represented these derivatives, [F3] would give $|\dot\psi_P(s_M)|=|P[\phi s_M]|\le\|\phi\|_2\|s_M\|_2$ for every $M$, contradicting step 1.3. Thus the mean functional has no square-integrable influence curve in this model, refuting the statement. [F2, F3, step 1.3, given] ∎

## Statement refuted

For fixed $M>0$, there are positive constants $C_M,c_0$ such that for every $p,n\ge1$ and $0\le\epsilon\le1$,
$$\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M)}\sup_Q P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}^{\otimes n}\left\{\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2\ge C_M\bigl((p/n)\vee\epsilon^2\bigr)\right\}\ge c_0,$$
where the infimum ranges over all Borel matrix-valued estimators.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a fixed $M>0$, proposed positive constants $C_M,c_0$, and the bounded-spectrum Gaussian Huber model.

[F1] [[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]]: every $\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M)$ is positive semidefinite with $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\le M$.

[F2] [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]: changing the sign of a matrix preserves its operator norm.

[F3] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the natural numbers are unbounded above in the real field.

[F4] [[def-huber-covariance-model]] gives the Gaussian Huber sample laws. Their Gaussian convention retains [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; the pointwise loss bound below is independent of the sampling law.

## Counterexample

1.1 The constant zero-matrix estimator is Borel, since the inverse image of any Borel set is either the entire sample space or empty. For every target in the class its squared operator loss is $\|0-\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2=\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2\le M^2$ by [F1]–[F2], for every possible observation and every contaminant. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], choose an integer $p>M^2/C_M$, and take $n=1$, $\epsilon=0$. The proposed threshold is $C_Mp>M^2$, so the tail event for the zero estimator is empty under every target and contaminant by step 1.1. Its worst-case probability, hence the nonnegative minimax infimum, is zero, contradicting $c_0>0$. Thus an uncapped all-dimension lower rate is false; the bounded loss requires a cap such as $\min\{1,(p/n)\vee\epsilon^2\}$ in a valid matching lower statement. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

For fixed $M>0$, there are positive constants $C_M,c_0$ such that for every $p,n\ge1$ and $0\le\epsilon\le1$,
$$\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M)}\sup_Q P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}^{\otimes n}\left\{\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2\ge C_M\bigl((p/n)\vee\epsilon^2\bigr)\right\}\ge c_0,$$
where the infimum ranges over all Borel matrix-valued estimators.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a fixed $M>0$, proposed positive constants $C_M,c_0$, and the bounded-spectrum Gaussian Huber model.

[F1] [[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]]: every $\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M)$ is positive semidefinite with $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\le M$.

[F2] [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]: changing the sign of a matrix preserves its operator norm.

[F3] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the natural numbers are unbounded above in the real field.

[F4] [[def-huber-covariance-model]] gives the Gaussian Huber sample laws. Their Gaussian convention retains [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; the pointwise loss bound below is independent of the sampling law.

## Counterexample

1.1 The constant zero-matrix estimator is Borel, since the inverse image of any Borel set is either the entire sample space or empty. For every target in the class its squared operator loss is $\|0-\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2=\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2\le M^2$ by [F1]–[F2], for every possible observation and every contaminant. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], choose an integer $p>M^2/C_M$, and take $n=1$, $\epsilon=0$. The proposed threshold is $C_Mp>M^2$, so the tail event for the zero estimator is empty under every target and contaminant by step 1.1. Its worst-case probability, hence the nonnegative minimax infimum, is zero, contradicting $c_0>0$. Thus an uncapped all-dimension lower rate is false; the bounded loss requires a cap such as $\min\{1,(p/n)\vee\epsilon^2\}$ in a valid matching lower statement. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and let
$(\epsilon_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be iid Rademacher variables
($P(\epsilon_t=1)=P(\epsilon_t=-1)=1/2$), and let $e(u)=1$ in
$H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$, so $\|e\|_H=1$. Let $N_0$ be the least
$N\in\mathbb N$ such that
$$\sum_{k>N}(k+1)^{-2}<1.$$
For $r\ge1$, recursively choose $N_r$ as the least integer greater than
$N_{r-1}$ such that
$$\sum_{k>N_r}(k+1)^{-2}<2^{-4r}.$$
Define a causal Borel filter by
$$f(x_0,x_1,\ldots)=e\lim_{r\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{N_r}\frac{x_k}{k+1}$$
when this subsequence converges, and define $f=0$ otherwise. Then
$X_t=f(\epsilon_t,\epsilon_{t-1},\ldots)$ is centered and has finite second
moment, but its physical-dependence coefficients satisfy
$$\delta_m^2=2\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac1{(k+1)^2},\qquad \delta_m\ge\sqrt{\frac{2}{m+1}}\quad(m\ge1).$$
Consequently $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m=\infty$: the sufficient summability
hypothesis in [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]] does not
apply to this shift. The example makes no claim that nonsummability alone
precludes every possible central limit theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countably many iid Rademacher innovations, the real Hilbert space $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$, and the replacement convention in [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]].

[F1] The countable product carrying iid Rademacher variables exists under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).

[F2] The scalar $L^2$ quotient is complete and its norm is induced by the integral inner product ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

[F3] Chebyshev's inequality bounds the probability of a deviation by its variance divided by the squared threshold, and the first Borel--Cantelli lemma makes events with summable probabilities occur only finitely often ([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]], [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

[F4] The stated two-point Rademacher law gives $\mathbb E\epsilon_t=0$ and $\mathbb E\epsilon_t^2=1$ by the expectation definition. Independence is the independence of the generated sigma-algebras ([[def-independent-random-elements]]); expectations of products of integrable functions of distinct independent coordinates factor ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]).

[F5] Cauchy--Schwarz on a probability space gives $\mathbb E|Y|\le\|Y\|_2$; thus $L^2$ convergence implies convergence of means and of $L^2$ norms ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

[F6] Since $x^{-2}$ is decreasing, $\sum_{j=2}^N j^{-2}\le\int_1^N x^{-2}\,dx\le1$, so $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}<\infty$. Since $x^{-1/2}$ is decreasing, $\sum_{j=2}^N j^{-1/2}\ge\int_2^{N+1}x^{-1/2}\,dx\to\infty$, so $\sum_{j\ge2}j^{-1/2}=\infty$.

## Proof

**Given:** The probability space and iid Rademacher innovations in the Statement, together with the independent replacement extension from [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]].

1.1 By [F6], the coefficient series $\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)^{-2}$ converges and its tails tend to zero. Hence the set defining $N_0$ is nonempty, so its least element exists. For $r\ge1$, once $N_{r-1}$ is chosen, the tail tends to zero, so some integer $N>N_{r-1}$ satisfies the required bound $\sum_{k>N}(k+1)^{-2}<2^{-4r}$; thus the least such $N_r$ exists. For a deterministic sign sequence $x=(x_k)_{k\ge0}$, put $s_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}x_k/(k+1)$. Each $s_N$ is product-measurable. The set on which $(s_{N_r})_{r\ge0}$ is Cauchy is Borel, because the Cauchy condition is a countable combination of inequalities between these measurable real functions. On that set their limit is measurable, and extending it by zero on the complement is product-measurable. Thus $f$ is a total Borel map into the one-dimensional subspace $\mathbb Re\subset H$. [given, F1, F6, construct, algebra]

2.1 On the given probability space carrying the iid innovations, the partial sums $S_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\epsilon_{-k}/(k+1)$ are Cauchy in $L^2$, since for $M>N$ independence, centering and [F4] give $$\mathbb E|S_M-S_N|^2=\sum_{k=N+1}^{M}(k+1)^{-2}\longrightarrow0.$$ By [F2] they converge in $L^2$ to a random variable $S$. Each $S_N$ has mean zero and squared norm $\|S_N\|_2^2=\sum_{k=0}^N(k+1)^{-2}$; [F5] therefore gives $\mathbb ES=0$ and $\mathbb ES^2=\|S\|_2^2=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}<\infty$ by [F6]. Choose increasing $N_r$ with $\sum_{k>N_r}(k+1)^{-2}<2^{-4r}$. Taking $M\to\infty$ in the finite tail-variance identity gives $\mathbb E|S_{N_r}-S|^2=\sum_{k>N_r}(k+1)^{-2}$. Thus [F3] gives $$P(|S_{N_r}-S|>2^{-r})\le 2^{2r}\mathbb E|S_{N_r}-S|^2<2^{-2r}.$$ These probabilities are summable, so [F3] implies $S_{N_r}\to S$ almost surely. Hence the defining subsequence filter equals $S e$ almost surely. In particular $X_0$ is centered and $$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2=\mathbb ES^2=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}<\infty.$$ The same argument applies to every shifted iid input sequence. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $m\ge1$, the mixed sequence used by $X_{0,m}$ is itself iid Rademacher, so its filter is the corresponding $L^2$ limit. Subtracting its partial sums from those for $X_0$ cancels the terms $k<m$ and leaves $$X_0-X_{0,m}=e\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_{-k}-\epsilon'_{0,m,-k}}{k+1} \quad\text{in }L^2.$$ The summands are independent, centered, and have variance $2/(k+1)^2$ by [F4]; finite-tail variance computation followed by $L^2$ convergence therefore gives $\delta_m^2=2\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $x\mapsto x^{-2}$ is decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, $$\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2} \ge\int_{m+1}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=\frac1{m+1}.$$ Thus $\delta_m\ge\sqrt{2/(m+1)}$, and the decreasing-function integral comparison gives $$\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m\ge\sqrt2\sum_{j\ge2}j^{-1/2}\ge\sqrt2\int_2^{\infty}x^{-1/2}\,dx=+\infty$$ by [F6]. The moment condition holds by step 2.1, but the required dependence-coefficient summability fails. [F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

[[thm-grouping-independent-sigma-algebras]]).

## Statement

Let $\mathcal C=C([0,1];H)$ with the supremum norm, choose a unit vector
$e\in H$, and define deterministic paths
$$w_{2r}(t)=0,\qquad w_{2r+1}(t)=\sin(\pi t)e\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
Every terminal value is zero, so the laws of $w_n(1)$ converge to the point
mass at $0$ in $H$. The laws of the paths do not converge weakly on
$\mathcal C$. This illustrates why the sample-sum CLT in
[[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]] is not a
time-indexed process CLT.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The metric space $\mathcal C$ with
$d(w,v)=\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|w(t)-v(t)\|_H$ and the deterministic paths in
the Statement.

[F1] Weak convergence of Borel probability laws entails convergence of
integrals of bounded continuous real functions ([[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]]).

[F2] The preceding Hilbert-valued theorem concerns normalized sample sums
as single $H$-valued random elements, not paths indexed by $t\in[0,1]$
([[thm-hilbert-valued-clt-for-l2-m-approximable-bernoulli-shifts]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The paths $w_n$ and their point-mass laws.

1.1 Since $\sin(0)=\sin(\pi)=0$, both even and odd paths satisfy $w_n(1)=0$. Thus their terminal laws are all the point mass $\delta_0$ and in particular converge weakly to $\delta_0$ in $H$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Define $\Phi:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R$ by $\Phi(w)=\min\{1,\sup_{0\le t\le1}\|w(t)\|_H\}$. The supremum norm inequality gives $$|\sup_t\|w(t)\|_H-\sup_t\|v(t)\|_H| \le\sup_t\|w(t)-v(t)\|_H=d(w,v),$$ and truncation by $x\mapsto\min(1,x)$ is 1-Lipschitz on $[0,\infty)$. Hence $\Phi$ is bounded and continuous. It equals $0$ on every even path and $1$ on every odd path, so its expectations under the path laws alternate between $0$ and $1$ and do not converge. By [F1], those path laws cannot converge weakly. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The example has convergence only after applying the terminal evaluation map; the bounded continuous path functional in step 1.2 detects the missing path-space convergence. Therefore endpoint convergence alone supplies no functional CLT conclusion, consistently with the scope in [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎
